questions.title: What is the difference between var, let and const?
questions.answer: var is function-scoped, while let and const are block-scoped. var can be redeclared, whereas let and const cannot be redeclared in the same scope. const requires initialization and prevents reassignment of its binding.
questions.underTheHood: All three declarations create bindings during environment initialization. var bindings are initialized to undefined, while let and const remain uninitialized until their declarations execute, creating the Temporal Dead Zone.
pitfalls: const does not make objects immutable.
var is function-scoped, not block-scoped.
Accessing let or const before initialization throws ReferenceError.
followUps: What is the Temporal Dead Zone?
Why should const generally be preferred?

questions.title: What is the difference between declaration, initialization and assignment?
questions.answer: Declaration introduces a binding. Initialization gives it its initial value. Assignment updates an existing binding.
questions.underTheHood: JavaScript establishes bindings during environment setup. Their initialization behavior depends on the declaration type.
questions.code:
let value; // Declaration, initialized to undefined
value = 10; // Assignment

const count = 5; // Declaration + initialization
pitfalls: const declarations must have an initializer.
An uninitialized let binding is different from a let binding initialized to undefined.

questions.title: What are primitive and reference types?
questions.answer: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol and null. Objects are non-primitive values. Primitive values are compared by value, while objects are compared by identity.
questions.underTheHood: Variables hold JavaScript values. When an object is assigned to another variable, both variables can refer to the same object. The exact memory representation is engine-dependent.
pitfalls: Arrays and functions are objects.
Objects are compared by identity, not structural equality.
typeof null returns 'object' due to historical behavior.
followUps: What are the seven primitive types?
What is the difference between shallow and deep copying?

questions.title: How does the typeof operator work?
questions.answer: typeof returns a string describing the type of its operand. It is useful for checking primitives and functions, but it cannot reliably distinguish arrays, null and ordinary objects.
questions.underTheHood: typeof is a language operator with predefined results for JavaScript values.
questions.code:
typeof 42; // 'number'
typeof 'hello'; // 'string'
typeof undefined; // 'undefined'
typeof null; // 'object'
typeof []; // 'object'
typeof (() => {}); // 'function'

Array.isArray([]); // true
pitfalls: typeof null is 'object'.
typeof [] is 'object'.
Use Array.isArray() to detect arrays.
followUps: What is the difference between typeof and instanceof?

questions.title: What is type coercion?
questions.answer: Type coercion is JavaScript's automatic conversion of values between types when an operation requires it. Explicit conversion occurs when developers intentionally call conversion functions such as Number() or String().
questions.underTheHood: Operators apply language-defined conversion algorithms. The + operator may perform string concatenation, while subtraction generally requires numeric conversion.
pitfalls: The + operator performs addition or concatenation.
Implicit conversions can produce unexpected results.
Number('abc') produces NaN.
followUps: What is implicit versus explicit conversion?
How does the + operator decide between addition and concatenation?

questions.title: What are truthy and falsy values?
questions.answer: Truthy values convert to true in Boolean contexts, while falsy values convert to false. Falsy values include false, 0, -0, 0n, an empty string, null, undefined and NaN.
questions.underTheHood: Conditions use JavaScript's ToBoolean conversion. Objects are truthy, including empty arrays and empty objects.
questions.code:
Boolean(0); // false
Boolean(''); // false
Boolean([]); // true
Boolean({}); // true
Boolean('false'); // true
pitfalls: Empty arrays are truthy.
Empty objects are truthy.
The string 'false' is truthy.
followUps: What is the difference between || and ??

questions.title: What is the difference between == and ===?
questions.answer: == performs loose equality comparison and may convert operands before comparing them. === performs strict equality comparison without type coercion.
questions.underTheHood: Loose equality follows the Abstract Equality Comparison algorithm. Strict equality follows the Strict Equality Comparison algorithm.
questions.code:
5 == '5'; // true
5 === '5'; // false
null == undefined; // true
null === undefined; // false
pitfalls: == can trigger implicit conversions.
NaN is not strictly equal to itself.
Two distinct objects are never strictly equal.
followUps: How does NaN behave during comparison?

questions.title: What is the difference between || and ??
questions.answer: || returns its right operand when the left operand is falsy. ?? returns its right operand only when the left operand is null or undefined.
questions.underTheHood: Both operators short-circuit and return an operand rather than necessarily returning a Boolean.
pitfalls: || treats zero and empty strings as fallback conditions.
?? only handles nullish values.

questions.title: What is the difference between for, for...in and for...of?
questions.answer: A traditional for loop provides explicit control over initialization, condition and update. for...in iterates enumerable string property keys. for...of iterates values produced by an iterable.
questions.underTheHood: for...of uses the iteration protocol through Symbol.iterator. for...in enumerates property keys, including eligible inherited keys.
pitfalls: for...in is usually not recommended for array iteration.
Ordinary objects are not iterable by default.
for...of works with arrays, strings, Maps and Sets.
